title: Estimating Teacher Impacts on Student Achievement: An Experimental Evaluation
research_question: Do non-experimental estimates of teacher effects on student achievement provide unbiased and accurate predictions of how much students' end-of-year test scores would differ if a given classroom were assigned one teacher rather than another? Additionally, how persistent are teacher impacts on student achievement over subsequent years?
data_description: The study combines administrative data from the Los Angeles Unified School District (LAUSD) covering grades 2-5 from spring 1999 through spring 2007. Pre-period observational data (1999-2000 through 2002-03) cover roughly 1,950 teachers in the participating schools, with an average of 42-47 student test-score observations per teacher. Experimental data come from school years 2003-04 and 2004-05 and include 78 pairs of elementary classrooms (156 classrooms, 3,194 students). Test outcomes use the Stanford 9 (1999-2002), the California Achievement Test (2003), and the California Standards Test (2004 onward), each standardized by grade and year. Additional variables include prior-year math/reading/language scores, race/ethnicity, free/reduced-price lunch, Title I, English-language status, gifted/special-education status, retention, school, grade, and calendar track. The unit of observation is the student, aggregated to classroom and classroom-pair levels.
institutional_context: LAUSD is one of the largest U.S. school districts, serving roughly 747,000 students across 689 schools. The setting was created through a collaboration with LAUSD's Program Evaluation and Research Branch, originally designed to evaluate teachers applying for National Board for Professional Teaching Standards certification. Within participating elementary schools, principals identified pairs of teachers in the same grade and calendar track—one National Board applicant and a comparison teacher with at least three years of experience—and prepared two class rosters such that the principal would be equally satisfied with either roster-teacher pairing. On a pre-specified date, the district centrally determined whether to swap the rosters between the two teachers in each pair. After roster assignment, no further intervention occurred; about 85% of students remained with their assigned teacher through year-end testing. This setting offers within-school, within-grade variation in teacher assignment that is unrelated to classroom composition.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.identification_strategy: IV — treatment = teacher assignment, control = non-assigned teachers; shock/instrument/cutoff = randomized teacher assignment

key_variables.control: non-assigned teachers or previous teacher assignments
key_variables.outcome: student achievement scores on standardized tests

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The study finds a positive impact of teacher quality on student achievement, indicating that better teacher assignments lead to improved student performance.
